title: Cittar pāṭalkaḷ (the songs of the Siddhars)
summary: The anthology of the Tamil Siddhars' songs, printed since the 19th c. under titles such as Cittar pāṭalkaḷ and Periya ñāṉakkōvai. It gathers Sivavākkiyar, Pattinattār, Pattirakiriyār, Pāmbāṭṭi, Iṭaikkāṭar, Kuṭampai, Aḻukaṇṇi, Kaṭuveḷi, Akappēy and others: songs on the inner yoga, the body, impermanence, the guru and Civam, and against caste, idols and ritual.

attribution.scholarly: a modern (19th–20th c.) printed anthology; contents and verse numbering vary between editions

scholarly.text: undetermined; the Siddhar song corpus is usually placed c. 1400–1800

title: Civavākkiyam (the songs of Sivavākkiyar)
summary: About five hundred verses in a swift eight-foot metre, the most radical of the Siddhar songs: the Lord dwells within; the planted stone does not speak; temples and tanks are within the mind; caste has no basis in flesh and bone; Vedic recitation and ritual without knowledge are empty; one famous verse denies that the dead are reborn.

scholarly.text: undetermined; the Siddhar song corpus is usually placed c. 1400–1800

title: Pāmpāṭṭic cittar pāṭalkaḷ (the songs of the snake-charmer Siddhar)
summary: Songs with the refrain 'āṭu pāmpē' ('dance, O snake!'), addressed to the snake: praise of Śiva and the guru, the impermanence and filth of the body, the uselessness of learning, caste and ritual for liberation, and the inner ascent. Later readers take the snake as the coiled power (kuṇṭali) within.

title: Kutampaic cittar pāṭalkaḷ (the songs of Kuṭampai)
summary: Thirty-two couplets (kaṇṇi), each asking 'why … , Kuṭampai?' ('ētukkaṭi kutampāy'): for one who has seen the true thing, the open space (veṭṭa veḷi) and the root, what need of charters, kaṟpam (rejuvenation), mantra, seals, yoga, hymns, rituals, fame or a house? A catalogue of means made redundant by realization.

title: Kaṭuveḷic cittar: Āṉantak kaḷippu (the Joy-song)
summary: A pallavi and thirty-four caraṇams in popular song form: 'Do no sin, O mind — tomorrow Yama in his anger will carry you off.' The body is a bubble on water; the mendicant who begged a pot for months danced and broke it; will karma go by visiting Kāśī or bathing in the Gaṅgā? Devotion is highest; the eight-limbed yoga; the many castes are one; avoid ganja and toddy, false garb and cruelty; seek the pure Vedānta space.

title: Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam (the wisdom of Tiruvaḷḷuvar)
summary: Nineteen verses ascribed to Tiruvaḷḷuvar as a Siddhar: invocation of Agastya and the coiled power; the body's impermanence; knowledge of the whirl (cuḻi) and the root; the Veda's essence as ghee in milk; kāya-siddhi removing karma; salt, 'muppu' and the vāci breath making the body endure.

title: Paṭṭiṉattār pāṭalkaḷ (Tiruppāṭal tiraṭṭu)
summary: The songs ascribed to the renouncer Paṭṭiṉattār (Tiruveṇkāṭar): the Tiruvēkampamālai to Śiva at Kāñcī, the Tillai verses, three Kōyil tiruvakavals, the Kacci tiruvakaval and the Aruṭpulampal, with further 'general' songs and the songs at his mother's cremation. Themes: impermanence, the body as a pot of filth, renunciation, women as snare, karma, and refuge in Śiva's feet.

tradition.text: the tradition makes the renouncer a merchant of Kāvirippūmpaṭṭiṉam in the Cōḻa age

scholarly.text: the Siddhar songs are usually placed c. 14th–17th c. and distinguished from Paṭṭiṉattup Piḷḷaiyār of the eleventh Tirumuṟai (c. 10th c.)

title: Pattirakiriyār: Meyññāṉap pulampal (lament for true knowledge)
summary: Two hundred and thirty-one couplets after an invocation, each asking 'when will the day come (ekkālam)?' — when will I burn the five senses, sleep without sleeping in Śiva-yoga, see women as mother, stop killing living beings, see the chiselled stone and moulded image as no ultimate thing, leave Vedānta and Veda to abide alone, give up ganja, opium and toddy, and know 'who am I, who are you'?

title: Tāyumāṉavar pāṭalkaḷ (the songs of Tāyumāṉavar)
summary: About 1,450 stanzas in some fifty-six sections (Paraparakkaṇṇi, Āṉantakkaḷippu, Tējōmayāṉantam, Ciṉmayāṉantakuru, Mauṉakuru vaṇakkam, Cittarkaṇam and others) praising the all-pervading Supreme (Paraparam), the silent guru and stillness (cummā iruttal); they join Vedānta and Śaiva Siddhānta in a 'harmony' (camaracam), warn that stilling the mind is harder than any power, and pray that all beings be happy.

title: Vināyakar akaval (Auvaiyār)

notes: Siddha affiliation is the tradition's; which Auvaiyār (several poets bear the name) is unsettled. Contents recalled.
